subject: VAL
label: Grade 10
task: Meet the outcome of every unit in Grade 10 Values and life skills, and keep one piece of evidence for each.
condition: A 36-week school year, 4 units, a teacher or guide, a learning book or device, and local examples in the local language first with English support.
standard: Each unit: at least 8 of 10 marks on a short task, with one line of reasoning for each answer. Course pass: no unit at 'Not yet' after one retry, and a pass in SA1 and SA2.

modules.title: Ethics and leadership
modules.outcome: take a role in a team and review it
modules.intro: In this unit you work on 'Ethics and leadership', taught in a way that is with notes, a worked line and a self-mark. The target is clear: take a role in a team and review it. You move from seeing it, to saying it, to doing it alone.
points: Listen and talk: hear a short story, text or example linked to 'Ethics and leadership' and say what it means in your own words.
Connect: name one place in your own day where it applies.
Use it: take a role in a team and review it. Practise with care and respect, in class and at home.
Reflect: what went well, what was hard, and one thing you will do next time.
modules.example: Solved: Ethical decision steps: facts, who is affected, options, which value each option meets, choose, review later. Method: Model run for 'Ethics and leadership'. A short text or story is read aloud. Learners say the main lesson in one sentence. In pairs they find one moment in school or home where this lesson would help. Each learner plans one small action for the week and tells it to a partner. At the end of the week they report back. What a good answer looks like: the lesson is in the learner's own words, the example is real and local, and the action is small enough to do. Content follows the approved local syllabus and is checked by a qualified teacher.
modules.activity: About 30 to 40 minutes of class work, then one short practice task for home. Keep evidence: a worked task and a corrected copy.
modules.standard: Take a role in a team and review it: at least 8 of 10 marks on a short task, with one line of reasoning for each answer.
steps: Step 1, Choose the role: A team of 5 builds a school recycling campaign. Mariam volunteers as coordinator, with roles: Mariam leads, Hamad does posters, Sara tracks data, Ali talks to staff, Dana writes the newsletter. Clear roles come first.

Step 2, Set ethical rules: The team agrees: credit everyone's work, tell the truth in data, listen to every idea, and ask permission before using photos of students. Four rules go on the first page of the plan.

Step 3, Make a fair plan: There are 3 weeks and 15 tasks. 15 divided by 5 members is 3 tasks each. Mariam assigns 3 tasks to every member, including herself, so the leader does not take the easy ones.

Step 4, Handle a conflict: Sara finds the recycling bins were only 60 percent full, not the 80 percent that the poster says. Hamad wants to keep 80 because it looks better. Mariam says the poster must show the true 60.

Step 5, Decision: The team uses 60 percent and writes 'Bins are 60 percent full; let's make it 80.' Honest data makes a stronger, trusted campaign. Hamad agrees after seeing that exaggerated numbers could cost the team their credibility.

Step 6, Review the role: Mariam asks each member to rate teamwork out of 5 on fairness, communication and honesty. Ratings 4, 5, 4, 4, 5 total 22, giving an average of 4.4. She writes one thing to improve: share deadlines earlier.
Your turn: Team of 4 scores 3, 4, 5, 4 for teamwork. Average and one lesson? Model answer: total 16, average 4.0; a lesson might be to check in halfway through, because the lowest score was 3.

modules.standard: Match strengths to career paths: at least 8 of 10 marks on a short task, with one line of reasoning for each answer.
steps: Step 1, List strengths: Khalid rates himself from 1 to 5: Numbers 5, Making things 4, Helping people 3, Writing 2. These come from real activities, such as maths club, building a robot kit, class mentoring and essay marks, not just wishes.

Step 2, Define career profiles: He lists what each career uses, as weights: Engineering 0.4 numbers, 0.4 making, 0.1 helping, 0.1 writing. Nursing 0.2, 0.1, 0.5, 0.2. Journalism 0.1, 0.1, 0.2, 0.6. Each set of weights adds up to 1.
Step 3, Score Engineering: 5 times 0.4 is 2.0; 4 times 0.4 is 1.6; 3 times 0.1 is 0.3; 2 times 0.1 is 0.2. Total is 2.0 plus 1.6 plus 0.3 plus 0.2, which equals 4.1 out of 5.
Step 4, Score the others: Nursing is 5 times 0.2 (1.0) plus 4 times 0.1 (0.4) plus 3 times 0.5 (1.5) plus 2 times 0.2 (0.4), which is 3.3. Journalism is 0.5 plus 0.4 plus 0.6 plus 1.2, which is 2.7.

Step 5, Read the results: Engineering 4.1 is highest, then Nursing 3.3 and Journalism 2.7. The gap suggests exploring engineering fields first. A score is a guide, not a verdict, because interests grow and the weights are rough.

Step 6, Next actions: He talks to an engineer, joins a design club, and checks the subjects needed for engineering courses. He keeps nursing as a second option and revisits the scores in a year. Real career choices include more than interest.

Your turn: Strengths: Numbers 3, Making 2, Helping 5, Writing 4. Use Nursing weights 0.2, 0.1, 0.5, 0.2. Model answer: 0.6 plus 0.2 plus 2.5 plus 0.8 is 4.1 out of 5, a strong match for helping careers.

modules.intro: In this unit you work on 'Civic responsibility', taught in a way that is with notes, a worked line and a self-mark. The target is clear: describe a citizen's duties in the UAE and globally. You move from seeing it, to saying it, to doing it alone.

Reflect: what went well, what was hard, and one thing you will do next time.
modules.example: Solved: Class jobs: Monday Asha waters plants, Tuesday Ben tidies books. A fair rule: everyone takes a turn, and everyone knows it in advance. Method: Model run for 'Civic responsibility'. A short text or story is read aloud. Learners say the main lesson in one sentence. In pairs they find one moment in school or home where this lesson would help. Each learner plans one small action for the week and tells it to a partner. At the end of the week they report back. What a good answer looks like: the lesson is in the learner's own words, the example is real and local, and the action is small enough to do. modules.activity: About 30 to 40 minutes of class work, then one short practice task for home. Keep evidence: a worked task and a corrected copy.
modules.standard: Describe a citizen's duties in the UAE and globally: at least 8 of 10 marks on a short task, with one line of reasoning for each answer.
steps: Step 1, Define the duties: Hind lists what citizens do: follow the law, respect other people and cultures, take part in the community, protect shared places and resources, and care about people beyond their own country. Rights go with these duties.

Step 2, Local case: In the school street, litter is common after lunch. Following the rules and keeping shared space clean is a duty. Hind and 5 friends collect litter for 10 minutes each day, which is 5 days times 10 minutes, so 50 minutes a week.

Step 3, Respect and law: A foreign visitor asks Hind for directions. She answers politely, in simple words, and she follows traffic rules when crossing. Respecting the law and treating guests kindly are both civic duties in her country.

Step 4, Participation: The school council asks for ideas on the canteen waste. Hind submits one clear idea, a sorting bin for paper and plastic, rather than only complaining. Taking part means contributing and accepting majority decisions.

Step 5, Global duty: Hind learns that wasted water is a shared global problem. She counts how long she runs the tap: 2 minutes twice a day, so 4 minutes. By turning it off while brushing she saves about 2 of those 4 minutes each day.

Step 6, Plan and review: She makes a week table with 3 local actions (litter, kindness, school council idea) and 2 global ones (water, waste). That makes 5 actions, and she ticks those she completed, honestly reporting 4 out of 5.

Your turn: List 2 local and 1 global duty you could do this week, with one measure. Model answer: keep the class tidy daily, greet a visitor politely, and turn the tap off while brushing; count days done out of 7.
